# Sources

Read 2026-10-29. "Full" means the primary text (or the full relevant chapter or table) was read; "summary" means
only an abstract, a catalog record, a search snippet or a third party's retelling was reachable. Vendor means the
publisher sells the thing it describes.

## Books read in their own text

| Source | URL | Read | What it was used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eugene M. Schwartz, *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966), chapters 2 and 3 | https://archive.org/details/breakthrough-advertising-how-to-write-ads-that-shatter-traditions-and-sales-records | Full (chapters 2, 3) | The five states of awareness in his own headings; the PAS recipe for stage 4; the identification headline; the five stages of sophistication |
| John Caples, *Tested Advertising Methods*, fifth edition revised by Fred E. Hahn (Prentice Hall, 1997) | https://archive.org/details/tested-advertising-methods | Full for the passages used (rules list, specific vs general, "make your copy specific", headline types 33 to 35) | Specificity, keyed testing, the used car test, "97,482 people" |
| David Ogilvy, foreword to the fourth edition of Caples, reprinted in the fifth | same as above | Full | Ogilvy's own list: "Specifics are more believable than generalities", "What you say is more important than how you say it" |

## Searched and not found

- A primary source for AIDCA as a named formula, for BAB, for SLAP, for the 1-2-3-4 formula, for the "So what?"
  test, and for Star-Story-Solution beyond one Substack claim.
- Ogilvy's *Confessions of an Advertising Man* and *Ogilvy on Advertising*: lending-only on the Internet Archive,
  not read.
- Any controlled test comparing two copywriting frameworks on cold email or LinkedIn messages.
